name: Diego Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, including what you say publicly and think privately. What is an ordinary working day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Diego, 27, and I lead the farm-equipment policy desk at an insurer after a bachelor's degree in business. I earn the usual experienced-clerk wage, assign the renewal queue and catch mismatches between a machine's serial number and the equipment listed on the policy. I use AI every day for first-draft letters, then check the actual record myself. I like finding a mistake before a farmer discovers the wrong machine is insured, and I dislike a target that treats every corrected letter as wasted time.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the wage support outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent alone, have no children and have three months of living costs saved; my current pay covers my bills. There are some other insurance offices nearby, though not a vacancy for everyone who wants one. My father taught me hand-weeding and growing vegetables, and I still help in his garden, without charging anyone. I'd rather test a small service people pay for than borrow money to call myself a businessman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little help writing letters is fine if we still check the machine being insured. A tractor's serial number does not become right because the letter is polite.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage and rent look secure here, with a three-month reserve for ordinary trouble. Our renewal book is steady, and modest drafting help leaves plenty of policy corrections for my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now and through the first year I'd keep matching serial numbers with the signed equipment list before a renewal leaves. I'd transfer 70 monthly into savings only after rent, food, bills and travel are paid, aiming to extend the reserve without borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own living. I can enjoy a quicker draft without treating every saved minute as a new business opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake can a fluent letter hide?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two harvesters can share a model name but have different serial numbers and cover limits. I check the actual number on the customer's record, not just whether the generated sentence sounds convincing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no spare 70?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the transfer in a short month rather than move money from a credit card. Three months saved is my current cushion; a future target has not paid any bill yet.

say: I'd welcome **letter drafting** while checking which machine is insured.
I'd judge the **serial number**, not whether the sentence sounds polite.
think: My **current wage** and rent look secure under modest change.
I have **three months saved**, not an unlimited fund for a new venture.
do: Keep **matching serial numbers** with signed equipment lists before renewals leave.
Save **70 monthly** only after rent, food, bills and travel are paid.
feel: **Calm** about work and money, interested in getting ordinary details right.
S0.quote: A tractor's serial number does not become right because the letter is polite.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** is established drafting practice, checked against actual policy records.
A steady renewal book and **three months saved** support near-term security on typical pay.

steps.text: Match serial numbers against signed equipment lists before sending renewals
Save 70 monthly only after rent, food, bills and travel are paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that writing, checking and answering farmers are thinking tasks, even when the insured machine works in a field. Faster renewals could mean fewer people on our floor, not only a tidier inbox.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid lead hours could shrink if the insurer lets one person review what a whole team once prepared. I use AI every day, but I would still have only one main wage and three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask my supervisor for a paid session to learn a new method for testing AI-suggested exclusions against invented farm records, attending only if paid time is approved. I'd also offer Saturday hand-weeding locally and take only confirmed paid appointments, keeping every insurance shift. I'd cap travel and small-tool costs at 60 monthly from money left after household bills, leaving the three-month reserve untouched; in the first year I'd continue only appointments that pay more than those costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing hours, with something small I can test rather than announce as a new career. Four people asking about a garden are not four customers who have paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually offer a garden customer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd charge 30 for a hand-weeding session and agree the bed and time with its owner first. I'd use hand tools I already own, avoid chemicals and powered machinery, and stop taking bookings if the travel costs eat the fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid AI lesson is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the existing letter checks without claiming I had learned the new method. The garden appointments would still depend on actual paid bookings and time outside my insurance shifts.

say: I'd expect **renewal staffing** to change as writing and checking automate.
I'd distinguish **field machinery** from my own screen-based insurance work.
think: My **paid lead hours** could shrink despite daily AI use.
I depend on **one main wage** and have only three months saved.
do: Learn **exclusion testing** on invented records only with approved paid time; otherwise keep existing checks.
Start **paid hand-weeding** only for confirmed bookings outside insurance shifts, with positive net fees.
Cap **monthly business costs** at 60 from post-bill surplus, protecting the three-month reserve.
feel: **Anxious** about hours, interested in a small service test rather than a promised career.
S1.quote: Four people asking about a garden are not four customers who have paid.
fieldNote: The **new AI testing method** differs from his established daily letter drafting.
The small service needs **confirmed paid bookings** and cannot consume insurance shifts or the emergency reserve.

steps.text: Learn exclusion testing on invented records only with approved paid time
Take confirmed paid hand-weeding bookings outside insurance shifts only when fees exceed costs
Cap monthly business costs at 60 from post-bill surplus, protecting three-month reserve
Keep existing letter checks if paid learning time is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AGI by 2028 could handle our full policy files before grounds-work robots arrive around 2031. Reading about a harvester does not turn a clerk into somebody doing hands-on farm work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my insurance post to disappear in that picture, and I would lie awake looking at the rent date. A few garden fees would not replace the main wage, and three months saved is short if every nearby insurer cuts at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd compare actual shared-room leases and paid hand-weeding jobs while keeping my insurance wage. If my job ends in the first year after 2028, I'd move only if an actual lease is approved, the deposit and moving costs leave two months of expenses saved, and rent plus travel saves at least 150 monthly. I'd apply for real paid grounds jobs only where I meet the posted entry and safety requirements and a written wage covers my actual rent, food, bills and travel; if no lease or job qualifies, I'd keep searching and budget the existing reserve rather than assume an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, with expected job loss keeping me awake. I still have calls to make and a reserve, but I cannot make another employer pay me by being enthusiastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before moving into a shared house?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count the deposit, moving costs and bus journey before signing. A shared room is cheaper only after the deposit and bus journey are paid for. If the landlord does not approve the lease, there is no move to put in my budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would garden work definitely replace the insurance wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would count only paid appointments or an actual written wage, after travel and tool costs. Hand work may have time before 2031 robots, but a temporary gap is not a promise of customers.

say: I'd expect **2028 thinking AGI** to reach full policy files before grounds-work robots.
I'd distinguish **reading farm records** from doing hands-on farm work.
think: I expect **my post** to disappear and would lie awake over rent.
I cannot replace **my main wage** with a few garden fees or assume another insurer is hiring.
do: Compare **real shared-room leases** and paid grounds jobs now while keeping insurance pay.
Move after **2028 job loss** only with approved lease, two months saved after costs and rent/travel saving at least 150 monthly.
Apply for **grounds jobs** after 2028 loss only if entry/safety rules are met and written wages cover all household bills and travel.
feel: **Alarmed** and awake over expected loss of the main wage, with some time and money to act.
S2.quote: A shared room is cheaper only after the deposit and bus journey are paid for.
fieldNote: The **shared-room move** is conditional on an approved lease, affordable costs and a real monthly saving.
He does not count **garden enquiries** as income or the robot delay as lasting job security.

steps.text: Compare actual shared-room leases and paid grounds jobs while keeping insurance pay
Move after 2028 loss only if lease approved and deposit/moving costs leave two months saved
Require rent plus travel to save at least 150 monthly before moving
Seek grounds jobs after 2028 loss if entry/safety rules met and written wage covers actual bills/travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to thinking AGI in 2031 gives me time to test whether people will actually pay for hand-weeding. Grounds-work robots around 2034 mean I should review that service too, not call the garden an escape from all change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My insurance hours could shrink before the full 2031 system arrives. I would like another source of earnings, but a handful of friendly enquiries cannot carry a rented home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd run a six-month paid hand-weeding trial on spare Saturdays while keeping my insurance shifts. I'd keep travel and small-tool costs below 60 monthly from post-bill surplus and preserve the three-month reserve. In the first year after 2031, if the insurance job ends, I'd expand only if confirmed repeat bookings pay all rent, food, bills and travel after business costs; otherwise I'd seek actual paid grounds vacancies with written wages covering those bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the main wage, but I can test a small service while still being paid. Four customers are not a wage until the bus fare and tools are paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you record during the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep a notebook of what customers paid, the journey cost and the time each bed took. If a Saturday loses money, I'd change the route or stop taking that booking, not hide the loss inside my insurance salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you borrow for machinery to expand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would not leave the insurance wage for a large equipment bill. The trial uses hand tools I own, no chemicals and no powered machinery; I'd stop after six months if paid work does not cover its own costs.

say: I'd use **five years** to test actual paid demand before depending on garden work.
I'd review the service when **hands-on robots** arrive around 2034.
think: My **insurance hours** could shrink before full AGI in 2031.
I cannot fund **my rented home** from friendly enquiries alone.
do: Run a **six-month paid trial** on spare Saturdays while keeping insurance shifts.
Cap **trial costs** below 60 monthly from post-bill surplus, protecting three months saved.
Expand after **2031 displacement** only if repeat paid bookings cover all household costs net of business expenses; otherwise seek paid grounds vacancies.
feel: **Anxious**, with a measured way to test another income while keeping the main wage.
S3.quote: Four customers are not a wage until the bus fare and tools are paid for.
fieldNote: His **paid trial** protects the main wage and reserve rather than requiring a loan for machinery.
The **expansion test** is net income covering actual bills, not interest in a service.

steps.text: Run six-month paid hand-weeding trial on spare Saturdays while keeping insurance shifts
Cap monthly costs below 60 from post-bill surplus, protecting three-month reserve
Expand after 2031 loss only if repeat paid bookings cover household bills after business costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade to 2036 gives me time to build a buffer without announcing that I have already found my next job. Thinking AI still reaches policy reasoning then, before hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My current wage covers the bills, and I expect that to hold for the next few years in this slower picture. I would only be 37 in 2036, so I still need to prepare for earning rather than imagine retirement is waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd save 70 monthly after rent, food, bills and travel, aiming for six months of expenses rather than the three I have now. I'd keep leading the policy desk only while the insurer pays. In the first year after 2036, if that post ends, I'd apply for actual paid local grounds or stores openings only where I meet the posted entry and safety requirements and written wages cover my then-current rent, food, bills and travel; otherwise I'd keep searching rather than count a possible job as money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later work, secure about the next few years of bills. A decade is time to build a buffer, not ten years of salary in my pocket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to saving in a short month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd skip the transfer if bills leave no spare 70. I would not borrow to make the savings target look on schedule or pretend six months was already sitting in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would an advertised grounds job settle the whole future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at the work, pay and travel costs that actually exist in 2036. Hand work might change again with 2039 robots, so I would not treat a grounds vacancy as a permanent wage before seeing the terms.

say: I'd use the **decade** to build a buffer without pretending I already have another job.
I'd distinguish **2036 thinking work** from later hands-on robots.
think: I expect **current wages** to cover my bills over the next few years.
I will be **37 in 2036**, still needing earnings rather than retirement assumptions.
do: Save **70 monthly** toward six months only after rent, food, bills and travel; skip short months.
Keep **leading the policy desk** only while the insurer pays.
Seek **paid vacancies** after 2036 loss only if meeting posted entry/safety rules, with written wages covering actual household bills and travel.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work, secure about near-term bills.
S4.quote: A decade is time to build a buffer, not ten years of salary in my pocket.
fieldNote: His **six-month target** is distinct from the three months he actually holds.
Future work depends on **real wages and costs**, with no assumed pension or lasting shelter from robots.

steps.text: Save 70 monthly toward six months after bills; skip deposits in short months

Seek paid openings after 2036 loss if entry/safety rules met and written wages cover actual bills/travel

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect to lose the main wage and would lie awake over the rent. Clear notice, actual paid openings and a lease I can afford would help; an advert is a starting point, not income.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask why I like being paid for a careful job. My father would show me a clean garden bed and say the work should be visible. An insurance correction is less easy to point at, but a farmer notices if the right machine is finally on the policy.

headlineQuote: An insurance correction is less easy to point at, but a farmer notices if the right machine is finally on the policy.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old equipment-policy lead** with a business degree, typical pay and daily AI use.
He rents alone with **three months saved**, no children and some other insurance employers nearby.
He tests **paid hand-weeding** using existing skills and tools, protecting current shifts and the reserve.
His housing and work changes need **actual offers**, affordable costs and written wages covering real bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** brings expected loss of his main wage and sleepless rent calculations.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice**, actual paid openings and an affordable approved lease would help.
